articles.title: Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stake
articles.summary: The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant test of Indian-American political representation.
articles.body: The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant test of Indian-American political representation.Four Indian-origin Democrats — Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam — are seeking re-election to the House of Representatives. Meanwhile, Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a high-octane race for governor of Ohio, and physician-turned-politician Amish Shah is attempting to capture an open Arizona congressional seat.Read also | US midterm elections 2026: Why it's a do-or-die fight for Trump & the Democracts - explained in 10 chartsThe contests extend beyond Congress. Indian-American candidates are competing for attorney-general positions, mayoralties and seats in state legislatures across the country.The elections on November 3 will take place against the backdrop of a closely divided Congress and a national debate over the economy, immigration, healthcare, technology and Trump's policies. The outcomes could determine not only which party controls Capitol Hill but also how much influence Indian-American lawmakers exercise in Washington and state governments.Indian-Americans in key congressional races1. Ro KhannaRo Khanna, one of the most prominent Indian-American Democrats in Congress at the moment, is seeking a sixth term from California’s 17th Congressional District, which covers much of Silicon Valley, including parts of Santa Clara and Alameda counties. He faces Republican Ritesh Tandon in the midterms, after comfortably finishing first in California’s June 2 nonpartisan primary with 62.3% of the vote. Tandon advanced with 14.8%.The district, home to major technology companies and a large population of technology workers, has consistently favoured Democrats.First elected to the House in 2016, Khanna has established himself as a progressive voice on economic policy, technology, foreign affairs and the role of American power overseas.Born in Philadelphia to Indian immigrant parents, he studied economics at the University of Chicago and earned a law degree from Yale University. Before entering Congress, he taught economics at Stanford University, practised law and served as deputy assistant secretary of commerce under President Barack Obama.He now sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has been an influential voice on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing to US competition with China.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Ro Khanna, Indian-American Congressman behind Epstein files pushKhanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies, immigration crackdown and approach to democratic institutions. He has challenged the administration’s priorities on taxation and economic inequality, arguing that government policy should benefit working families rather than disproportionately favour wealthy individuals and corporations. His opposition to Trump also extends to the president’s use of executive power and his approach to foreign policy, where Khanna has advocated greater congressional oversight of military action and a stronger emphasis on diplomacy.At the same time, Khanna has sought to distinguish himself from the Democratic establishment by championing a more populist economic agenda, including investment in manufacturing, clean energy, education and healthcare.His views on technology, economic inequality and America’s global role frequently place him at the centre of the party’s policy debate.2. Pramila JayapalPramila Jayapal is seeking re-election from Washington’s 7th Congressional District, which includes much of Seattle and surrounding communities. She faces Republican Nirav Sheth in the midterms after dominating the state’s nonpartisan primary, securing 84.4% of the vote against Sheth’s 9.8%.The result underlined her strong standing in a heavily Democratic district, where she has built a substantial political base through her advocacy on immigration, healthcare and economic inequality.Elected to Congress in 2016, Jayapal made history as the first South Asian American woman elected to the House of Representatives.Born in India, she moved to the United States at 16 to attend Georgetown University and later earned an MBA from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, she founded OneAmerica, a Washington-based immigrant-rights organisation, and became a prominent campaigner for immigration reform and civil liberties. Her experience as an activist has shaped her legislative priorities, particularly on deportations, detention, family separation and pathways to legal status.Jayapal has championed Medicare for All, stronger labour protections, affordable housing, climate action and expanded access to education. She has also held leadership positions in the Congressional Progressive Caucus and serves on the House Judiciary, Foreign Affairs and Budget committees, giving her influence over debates on immigration enforcement, federal spending and American foreign policy.Read also | US midterms 2026: From immigration reform to $15 minimum wage, all about Pramila JayapalA vocal critic of President Donald Trump, Jayapal has repeatedly challenged his administration’s immigration crackdown, deportation policies and restrictions on legal immigration. She has argued that the administration’s approach threatens civil liberties and undermines protections for immigrant communities. Her opposition also extends to Trump’s economic agenda and broader use of executive power, with Jayapal advocating stronger social protections and greater accountability for the administration.Her politics frequently put her to the left of the Democratic leadership, although she has worked within the party to advance progressive priorities.3. Ami BeraAmi Bera, one of the longest-serving Indian-American members of Congress, is seeking another term in California’s 3rd Congressional District, which covers Sacramento County and surrounding communities. He faces Republican Robb Tucker in the November 3 midterm elections.In the state’s nonpartisan primary, Bera secured 34.3% of the vote against Tucker's 29.9%.His re-election bid comes as Democrats seek to regain control of the House, with the Sacramento region offering a test of whether his established local support can withstand the broader national political climate.First elected in 2012, Bera has represented the Sacramento area in Congress since January 2013. The son of Indian immigrants, he grew up in California and earned his medical degree from the University of California, Irvine. Before entering politics, he worked as a physician and served as Sacramento County’s chief medical officer.His background has helped shape his political identity as a pragmatic Democrat who emphasises healthcare, public services and evidence-based policymaking rather than the more sweeping economic agenda associated with the party’s progressive wing.Read also | US midterms 2026: Who is Ami Bera, Indian-American Democrat seeking re-election from California's newly redrawn districtHealthcare remains a central part of Bera’s political profile. He has advocated improving access to medical care, reducing prescription drug costs and strengthening Medicare, while also focusing on education, infrastructure, veterans’ services and economic development. His approach generally favours targeted reforms and bipartisan cooperation, positioning him closer to the Democratic Party’s moderate wing on several policy questions.Foreign affairs, however, have become one of his defining areas of influence.Bera has served on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, with a particular interest in the Indo-Pacific. He has supported stronger US engagement with India and closer cooperation with regional partners, while emphasising the strategic challenge posed by China. His work has given him a prominent role in debates over US-India relations, regional security, intelligence oversight and the future of American engagement in Asia.4. Suhas SubramanyamSuhas Subramanyam is seeking a second term in the US House of Representatives from Virginia’s 10th Congressional District, which includes Loudoun County and parts of the surrounding Northern Virginia suburbs. He faces Republican Dave Beckwith and independent candidate Ahsen Mujeeb Malik in the midterms.The district, home to technology professionals, federal employees and government contractors, has generally favoured Democrats, but the Trump administration’s cuts to the federal workforce and changes to government spending have made these issues particularly consequential for local voters.Subramanyam entered Congress in January 2025 after defeating Republican Mike Clancy in the 2024 election. His victory made him one of the newest Indian-American members of the House. Born in Houston to Indian immigrant parents, he studied at Tulane University and earned a law degree from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, he worked with technology startups and served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House. He was elected to Virginia’s House of Delegates in 2019, becoming the first South Asian American elected to the state legislature, and later served in the Virginia Senate before moving to Congress.His political profile combines technology policy, economic affordability and a focus on practical local concerns. During his time in the Virginia legislature, he worked on issues including utility bills, prescription drug costs, education and gun safety. In Congress, he has emphasised support for small businesses, infrastructure investment, healthcare access and protecting federal workers. His background in technology has also shaped his attention to the rapid expansion of data centres in Northern Virginia, where new developments promise investment and jobs but raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, land use and higher infrastructure costs.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Suhas Subramanyam, Indian-origin Democrat who served as advisor to Barack ObamaSubramanyam has been critical of Trump’s policies on federal employment and government restructuring, arguing that abrupt cuts and uncertainty can harm public services and communities that depend on government jobs. His district is particularly exposed to such changes because of its concentration of federal agencies, contractors and defence-related businesses. He has also advocated reproductive healthcare protections, stronger gun-safety measures and policies aimed at lowering household expenses.New entrantsAmish Shah is running as the Democratic nominee in Arizona's 1st Congressional District. He previously contested the seat in 2024, losing to Republican David Schweikert. Schweikert is now running for governor, leaving the congressional seat open. Shah won the July 21, 2026, Democratic primary with 39.4% of the vote, defeating Marlene Galán-Woods, who received 34.4%. He faces Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, in November. The district is competitive, making this one of the more consequential races involving an Indian-origin congressional candidate. A FirstStrategic poll conducted on October 1 found Shah at 44.4% and Feely at 41.6% among registered voters, with a margin of error of 5.4 percentage points. A forecast updated October 23 projects Shah at 63% to win.Read also|US midterms 2026: Meet Amish Shah, the doctor seeking a second shot at CongressPia Dandiya is the Democratic nominee in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, an open seat where she faces Republican Casey Askar. Dandiya won the August 18 Democratic primary with 68.6% of the vote, defeating Kaysia Earley. Askar won the Republican primary with 30.9% in a crowded field.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Pia Dandiya, Indian-origin Democrat running for Florida’s open 22nd House seatRitesh Tandon is the Republican nominee challenging Khanna in California's 17th Congressional District. He advanced through the June 2 top-two primary with 19,793 votes, or 14.8%, finishing behind Khanna. The district is heavily Democratic, and current forecasts show Khanna with a substantial projected advantage.Nirav Sheth is the Republican challenger to Jayapal in Washington's 7th Congressional District. He secured second place in the state's nonpartisan primary, receiving 21,282 votes, or 9.8%. Jayapal won 84.4%. Sheth's advance means the November ballot will feature two races where Indian-origin candidates are facing off from opposing parties.Indian-American politicians not on the ballot Raja Krishnamoorthi lost the Democratic primary for the Illinois Senate seat and will not be the party's nominee in the November Senate election. His absence removes a high-profile Indian-American candidate from one of the year's most prominent Senate contests.Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary for Michigan's 13th Congressional District and is not the Democratic nominee in the November race.Gubernatorial race attracting national attention: Vivek RamaswamyVivek Ramaswamy, the Indian-American entrepreneur who emerged as a prominent voice in the Republican Party during the 2024 presidential race, is seeking to become governor of Ohio, the state where he was born and raised. The Republican nominee faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health. The contest has become a closely watched test of Ramaswamy's transition from conservative political outsider to candidate for executive office.Born in Cincinnati to Indian immigrant parents, Ramaswamy studied biology at Harvard University and law at Yale. He made his fortune in biotechnology and investment management, founding Roivant Sciences in 2014. His 2021 book, Woke, Inc., established his political identity as a critic of corporate diversity initiatives, environmental, social and governance investing and what he considers excessive ideological influence over business.During the 2024 Republican presidential primary, he advocated cutting government bureaucracy, restricting federal spending and challenging established political institutions. Although he withdrew from the race and endorsed Donald Trump, his combative campaign style helped establish him as a nationally recognised conservative figure.Trump subsequently selected Ramaswamy to co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency initiative alongside Elon Musk, although he left before the initiative's major restructuring efforts as he turned to the Ohio governor's race.His gubernatorial platform centres on reducing government costs, deregulation, education reform and expanding economic opportunity. His political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign, even as he seeks to establish an independent record as a candidate for state leadership.The campaign has recently been embroiled in controversy over an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother criticising her daughter.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Vivek Ramaswamy, Trump-backed Republican seeking the Ohio governorshipThe ad drew bipartisan condemnation, including from DeWine, who urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it. Trump, however, defended the advertisement and encouraged Ramaswamy to continue running it, while Vice-President JD Vance also criticised Republicans who opposed it. The dispute has sharpened questions about the role of personal attacks in the campaign and whether the controversy could affect Ramaswamy's standing with voters.Polling has shown Acton ahead, although the size of her lead varies. The RealClearPolling average for October 19 put Acton at 48.7% and Ramaswamy at 44.3%, while a Fox News poll conducted October 15–19 found a narrower 50-48 margin.Other statewide contestsNirav Shah, a physician and public-health administrator, is the Democratic nominee for governor of Maine. He previously served as director of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention from 2019 to 2023 and as principal deputy director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 2023 to 2025. Shah won Maine's June 9 Democratic gubernatorial primary with 26.9% of the vote.Aruna Miller, Maryland's lieutenant governor, is seeking to continue in office on the Democratic ticket led by Governor Wes Moore. Born in India, Miller immigrated to the US as a child and built a career as a transportation engineer before entering politics. Her career includes service in Maryland's House of Delegates and election as lieutenant governor in 2022. Miller's political position differs from that of a standalone gubernatorial candidate: the lieutenant governor runs on a joint ticket with the governor. Her electoral prospects therefore depend on the performance of the ticket as a whole as well as her own profile.Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-American Democrat Aruna Miller seeks re-election as Maryland Lt Governor alongside Wes MooreSaritha Komatireddy, a Republican lawyer and former federal prosecutor, is the Republican nominee for New York attorney general. She is challenging Democratic incumbent Letitia James. Her campaign offers Republicans an opportunity to contest an office that has become nationally prominent because of high-profile investigations and litigation involving major businesses and political figures.Read also | US midterms 2026: How 9/11 shaped Saritha Komatireddy’s legal career as she runs for New York attorney generalJosh Kaul, Wisconsin's Democratic attorney general, is seeking re-election.Nithya Raman: Running for Los Angeles mayorRaman is a Los Angeles City Council member and urban planner seeking to unseat Mayor Karen Bass. Her campaign focuses on housing, homelessness, city services and the cost of living. She has become a prominent figure in the city's progressive political movement.Raman advanced to the November 3 mayoral runoff after the June 2 primary. Certified results gave incumbent Bass 34.3%, Raman 29.0% and Spencer Pratt 25.5%. Raman's advance to the runoff turned the race into a direct contest between two Democrats.Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-born Nithya Raman challenges LA mayor Karen BassA McLaughlin & Associates/California Post poll conducted October 15–18 put Raman ahead by 7.9 percentage points. An Impact Research poll conducted October 2–7 put her ahead by 10 points, while a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies/Los Angeles Times poll from September 15–20 showed an 11-point lead.Raman's candidacy is significant beyond her own electoral prospects: a victory would make her the first South Asian woman to serve as Los Angeles mayor. Her campaign will test whether her progressive coalition can expand sufficiently to defeat an incumbent in a city facing persistent housing and homelessness challenges.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();What's at stake for Indian-AmericansFor the Indian-American community, the November 3 midterms are about more than individual victories. They are a test of how far a once-underrepresented community has come in American politics — and whether its growing presence can translate into greater influence in Congress, state governments and the national debate.The stakes are particularly high for the so-called ‘Samosa Caucus’, the informal label for Indian-American lawmakers in the US Congress.Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are fighting to retain their House seats, while challengers such as Amish Shah and Dandiya are seeking to expand the community’s footprint on Capitol Hill. Their outcomes will help determine whether Indian-origin representation in Congress consolidates, grows or faces a setback at a time when immigration, technology, healthcare, economic opportunity and America’s role in the world are fiercely contested.The stakes extend beyond Washington. Vivek Ramaswamy’s bid for governor of Ohio could take an Indian-American politician from national prominence to one of the country’s most powerful state offices. Nirav Shah’s campaign in Maine adds another dimension to the contest for statewide leadership. Success in races such as these would signal that Indian-origin candidates are competing not just in safe districts or within established political networks, but for executive power and leadership across the political map.Yet there is no single Indian-American political story. The candidates span the ideological spectrum — from progressive Democrats to more centrist lawmakers and conservative Republicans — and are campaigning on sharply different visions of government. Their fortunes will reflect not only the strength of their personal brands and local coalitions, but also how voters respond to their parties, their policies and the national political climate. Representation, in other words, does not automatically translate into a common agenda.Ultimately, November 3 will test whether Indian-American candidates can turn growing political visibility into electoral power. The results will shape not only the careers of individual candidates, but also the scale and reach of Indian-American representation in American public life — and the influence the next generation may be able to wield in setting the country’s political priorities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after leaving Brazil following election defeat to Lula
articles.summary: Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has arrived in the United States.
articles.body: Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has arrived in the United States.The 45-year-old landed in Miami, Florida, with his wife and two daughters, 48 hours after refusing to concede defeat. Bolsonaro secured 48% of the vote against Lula’s 52% and subsequently threatened to seek to “annul” the election results.Earlier, flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed that an aircraft matching Bolsonaro’s plane landed in Guayaquil, Ecuador, at around 4 am local time before departing minutes later for Miami’s Opa-locka Executive Airport. It had not been immediately clear at the time whether the defeated candidate was on board.From Brazil to US via Argentina and EcuadorAccording to Argentina’s migration authority, Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, entered Argentina at 10:50 pm local time on Tuesday with his wife, Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and their daughters, Carolina and Luiza. They crossed via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a key border crossing linking Brazil with Argentina’s northeastern province of Misiones.“Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country,” Argentina’s migration authority said in a post on X.At 11:30 pm, shortly after clearing immigration, the family boarded a private charter flight operated by Baires Fly SA, which, according to its filed flight plan, was headed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.Bolsonaro’s move is likely to strain relations between a newly re-elected Lula and his Argentine counterpart Javier Milei, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. Milei had travelled to Brazil to campaign for Bolsonaro.Why Flavio Bolsonaro left BrazilBolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court in two cases involving alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. The court had ordered him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports by noon on Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied, though he reportedly also holds an Italian passport.The senator received the Supreme Court order to hand over his Brazilian passports on Monday, according to a video in which he recounted being served the notice outside the home where his father is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest. Jair Bolsonaro attempted a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.Following that defeat, the former president fled to Florida before returning to Brazil three months later.In a video posted on Monday, Flavio Bolsonaro said he was seeking to rally fellow lawmakers against his defeat to Lula. Bolsonaro had won the first round of voting but failed to secure the 50% of votes required for an outright victory, triggering a run-off that Lula won to secure a fourth non-consecutive term.Flavio Bolsonaro’s eight-year Senate term expires on January 31, 2027, after which he will also lose the special jurisdiction that allows cases involving him to be heard by Brazil’s Supreme Court.Trump backs Flavio BolsonaroMeanwhile, Trump remarked early Wednesday (local time) that he would “approve” of Flavio Bolsonaro coming to the United States, describing the Brazilian senator and his family as “fine people”.“The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland after returning from a campaign event in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate but made clear that he did not endorse the election results.(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A UK charity collected 88,544 unwanted Christmas trees and recycled them into mulch, biomass and other uses, while the 2026 campaign raised £1.88 million for charities and helped support local communities
articles.summary: A UK charity collected 88,544 unwanted real Christmas trees after the festive season.
articles.body: A UK charity collected 88,544 unwanted real Christmas trees after the festive season. It turned them into reusable mulch, biomass and land management products. The effort also raised a record £1,885,915 for local causes. Just Helping, the national group behind the yearly Big Christmas TreeCycle Appeal, confirmed in its 2026 impact report that this was the largest campaign in its 14-year history. The total raised is £345,000 more than the year before. More than 4,000 volunteers gave their time to clear trees from streets across the UK. Under the scheme, households book a collection for their used trees and give a voluntary donation. The trees are taken to local processing hubs. There they are chipped and reused instead of being dumped in landfill. Data in the charity’s annual report shows that 81.2 pence of every pound raised went straight to 70 lead charity partners. Most of these are local hospices that organise the collection routes in their areas. Another 5.6 pence of every pound went to smaller local community groups. Just Helping kept 13.1 pence to pay for operating software, logistics and future growth.Nationwide reach and local community fundingThe 2026 scheme grew to reach more than 12 million households across the country. That is 3 million more homes than in 2025. Local hospice partners received £1,479,271 to support palliative care and community health services. A further £114,675 went to 109 smaller community groups, sports clubs, youth groups and food banks. These groups provided volunteers, vehicles and local know-how during the January pickup period. Just Helping founder Nick Stammers praised the thousands of people who helped with logistics, drove vans and chipped trees in the cold. “Every year, I’m reminded that the true strength of the Appeal isn’t measured by the number of trees collected or the funds raised, but by the extraordinary people who make it happen,” Nick Stammers said in a statement with the report. “To every volunteer, charity partner, supporter and corporate partner, thank you. Together you’ve helped strengthen communities, protect our environment and raise vital funds for local causes across the UK.” The Christmas TreeCycle scheme began in 2012 as a small local project. Since then, it has raised almost £9 million for UK charities. It has grown into a nationwide environmental and charity operation.Environmental benefits of diverting wood wasteCalculations in the report show that collecting and processing the 88,544 trees prevented an estimated 1.4 million kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions. When a standard two-metre real Christmas tree ends up in landfill, it breaks down slowly and gives off methane. This creates about 16 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions. Recycling the same tree cuts those greenhouse gas emissions by about 80 per cent, to around 3.5 kilograms. According to Just Helping, the carbon savings from the 2026 campaign equal driving an average petrol car more than 6 million miles. That is the same as going around the Earth more than 240 times. The shredded trees were made into woodchips for local parks, public gardens and community spaces. Other parts became biomass fuel for industry or were used in farm land management projects. To cut the carbon footprint of the collections themselves, the charity teamed up with corporate supporters to bring in electric vehicles. Healthcare firm Bupa sponsored 20 electric vans supplied by vehicle rental company Enterprise. These worked alongside fleet support from waste management firm Biffa during collections in Greater Manchester.High-profile support and future expansionThe 2026 campaign also got more public attention. Outdoor ads ran on 13 high-profile billboard sites in Greater Manchester and drew an estimated 12.5 million views. The appeal appeared on national television for the first time, when Nick Stammers was interviewed live on Sky News. Well-known figures also backed the campaign online. They included actor Mark Bonnar, TV presenter Alex Jones, former Strictly Come Dancing judge Dame Arlene Phillips and actor Lisa Riley. Just Helping said it plans to expand the scheme to more local authority areas and hospice catchments before the next festive season. Its goal is to make tree recycling available to more people across the UK.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Happy Karwa Chauth 2026: Images, Wishes, Messages, Quotes, Pictures and Greeting Cards
articles.summary: Karwa Chauth is a festival you can see, smell and hear before it even begins.
articles.body: Karwa Chauth is a festival you can see, smell and hear before it even begins. There is the henna drying on palms, the jingle of new bangles, the aroma of sargi in the pre-dawn kitchen, and the long, quiet wait for the moon. Greetings pour in from mothers-in-law, sisters, friends and colleagues, along with a flood of pictures and cards. Karwa Chauth falls on Thursday, October 29, 2026, in India, with moonrise in Delhi in the evening at around 8:17 pm. Puja and moonrise timings vary by city, and some calendars list October 28, so please check your local panchang. If you want your greetings to feel heartfelt rather than forwarded, here is a collection of wishes, messages, quotes and picture ideas that you can use as they are or tweak with a name and a memory of your own.Heartfelt wishes for everyoneThese all-purpose greetings suit relatives, neighbours and friends. articles.title: Citing diversion of staff from relief work, Maharashtra govt puts off cooperative society polls in all 304 drought-hit talukas
articles.summary: Maharashtra postpones cooperative society elections in 304 drought-hit talukas to avoid diverting staff from relief work; housing and court-ordered polls exempt.
articles.body: Mumbai: The state govt late on Tuesday indefinitely postponed elections for all eligible cooperative societies in the 304 talukas hit by drought, citing the need to prevent the diversion of administrative staff from relief work and inconvenience to farmers and others affected by the crisis.But cooperative housing societies, societies whose elections have been ordered by Supreme Court or Bombay high court, and those where the nomination process had begun before Tuesday have been exempted, according to a govt resolution (GR) issued by the state cooperation department.The state had seen feverish preparations for these elections over the past few months. All district central cooperative banks, which are considered the financial power centres of taluka and district politics, were scheduled to go to the polls, as were around 5,000 cooperative societies, like cooperative sugar factories, credit unions, cooperative banks, spinning mills, market committees and marketing associations. Last week, Rajarshi Shahu Shetkari Samavichari Aghadi, backed by Congress MLC Satej Patil, won the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers Federation polls with 13 seats, defeating the Mahayuti-supported Chhatrapati Shahu Shetkari Vikas Aghadi, led by senior NCP minister Hasan Mushrif, which secured 12 seats.The GR said owing to the drought situation in the 304 talukas, it is necessary to immediately implement various relief measures. “For this, additional administrative responsibility has been created on the revenue, agriculture, animal husbandry, cooperation, rural development, water supply, water conservation and other related departments. In such a situation, if the election process of cooperative societies in these talukas is continued, there is a possibility that govt officials/employees will get involved in the election process, which is likely to affect the drought relief work. Also, it is likely that it will be inconvenient for farmers and members of the drought-affected areas to participate in the election process of cooperative societies at the present time,” it said.The department invoked Section 73CC of Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, which empowers the state govt to defer cooperative elections during natural calamities and other exceptional circumstances.The state govt has announced relief measures for the 304 talukas. These include crop loan restructuring, suspension of agricultural loan recoveries, waivers on current electricity bills for agricultural pumps, provision of drinking water via tankers, fodder availability for livestock, and expanded employment under the employment guarantee scheme. articles.title: Bengal’s new industry policy may fast-track projects over 100 acres
articles.summary: Bengal’s new industry policy, to be unveiled Nov 5, aims to fast-track clearances for 100+ acre projects, tighten land-use rules and add investor incentives.
articles.body: Kolkata: Bengal’s new industry policy is expected to fast-track clearances for industrial projects requiring more than 100 acres and impose stricter conditions on land use. Chief minister Suvendu Adhikari will unveil the policy on Nov 5.The state cabinet approved the policy on Wednesday after incorporating recommendations from ministers. Industry captains have been invited to Nabanna for the launch.“The industry policy was discussed at the previous cabinet meeting. Recommendations from two ministers who were part of the Group of Ministers constituted to frame the policy were incorporated,” Adhikari said, crediting finance minister Swapan Dasgupta and industry minister Tapas Roy. “I have not interfered much in the formulation of the policy,” he added.According to Nabanna sources, the policy is expected to offer incentives to investors, streamline industrial clearances through a single-window system and introduce conditions governing the allocation and use of land for industrial projects.Govt is also considering a provision requiring industries to begin production within three years of receiving land, failing which allotments could be cancelled and land reclaimed. The final provisions will be known when the policy is formally unveiled.The policy is expected to be a key component of BJP govt’s efforts to improve Bengal’s investment climate and attract large-scale industrial projects.Adhikari also announced that financial assistance under Mukhyamantri Kisan Samman Nidhi, renamed from the earlier Krishak Bandhu scheme, would be transferred to farmers on Nov 5. He will initiate the transfer at a programme in Pursurah, Hooghly, which is expected to cover more than 50 lakh registered farmers.The cabinet also directed the finance department to release the next instalment of budgetary funds to administrative departments that have spent at least 70% of their allocations on public welfare schemes.It also approved observance of Janjatiya Gaurav Divas across Bengal from Nov 11 to 18 to commemorate the birth anniversary of tribal freedom fighter Birsa Munda.InsetState clears 1,200 posts across five departmentsThe state govt has approved around 1,200 new posts across five departments, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Wednesday. The posts have been approved in animal resources development, urban development and municipal affairs, health and family welfare, fire and emergency services, and home and hill affairs. “We will issue recruitment notifications soon and conduct examinations through PSC and SSC to fill these posts,” Adhikari said.He added that the state cabinet had approved around 45,000 posts at its previous meeting. articles.title: Sandalwood theft up, call for inquiry gets louder
articles.summary: Sandalwood theft rises in Palakkad’s Nenmara division as nine trees are felled in Thekkady; trust urges independent inquiry, case review and accountability.
articles.body: Palakkad: Heavy rain may have provided cover for the theft of sandalwood trees from the Thekkady forest station limits under the Kollengode forest range on Sunday.The forest department has registered a case after nine sandalwood trees were found to have felled in Vattayarmadakku forest, which comes under Nenmara forest division near Tamil Nadu border.Range officer V Unnikrishnan said the stolen timber may have been transported across the border into TN. Residents of a colony adjoining the forest are also under the scanner as part of the investigation.A detailed inspection carried out on Wednesday found that of the nine felled trees, six had been removed while two were abandoned because they lacked heartwood, according to forest officials.The incident has triggered concerns over repeated sandalwood thefts and illegal tree felling in the Nenmara forest division.Around 30 sandalwood trees have been reportedly stolen from Vamala and Thekkady in the past two months. In another incident, about 25 trees, including five sandalwood trees, were allegedly felled at Kottamala last week.The last sandalwood theft case registered at Thekkady forest station was in 2024, when 21 trees were stolen, Unnikrishnan said.Animals and Nature Ethics Community trust has urged the state govt to order an independent, time-bound inquiry into the incidents. It has sought a review of sandalwood theft cases registered over the past five years, scrutiny of forest patrol records and accountability for any established lapses.The organisation has also called for an investigation into an earlier tree-felling incident at Vattayarmadakku, during which some forest personnel were reportedly suspended around two years ago.The trust has demanded a written action-taken report detailing investigation progress, recoveries and arrests.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: Kamala Harris warns Democrats against third Trump impeachment, urges focus on investigations
articles.summary: Former US vice president Kamala Harris has urged Democrats against pursuing a third impeachment of President Donald Trump if they regain control of the
articles.body: Former US vice president Kamala Harris has urged Democrats against pursuing a third impeachment of President Donald Trump if they regain control of the House of Representatives in next week’s midterm elections, arguing that the party should focus on investigations and holding the administration accountable instead.According to the New York Post, Harris made the remarks during a Tuesday interview with MeidasTouch host Aaron Parnas, saying Democrats had limited resources and should avoid spending them on another impeachment effort.“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you,” Harris said, adding that the party’s time and resources should be directed towards “accountability” and “investigations”.Harris, who served in the Senate during Trump’s first term and as vice president during his second impeachment trial, also questioned whether Democrats would have enough votes to secure a conviction. “Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round, and the votes aren’t there,” she said.However, she urged Democrats not to soften their opposition to Trump, calling for an uncompromising approach focused on delivering results after the election. Harris said Democrats should prioritise getting things done rather than engaging in another prolonged political battle.“They’re ruthless, but they’re cruel. And when I say we should be ruthless, I don’t mean cruel, but we should be uncompromising,” she said.Trump was impeached twice during his first term. In December 2019, the Democratic-controlled House impeached him over his dealings with Ukraine, including allegations involving military aid and pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Senate acquitted him in February 2020.In January 2021, the House impeached Trump for a second time, accusing him of inciting the January 6 Capitol riot. The Senate again acquitted him, with Harris serving as vice president during the trial.House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has not ruled out another impeachment effort if Democrats win control of the chamber. He has said the party has “not ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out”, while indicating that other administration officials, including War Secretary Pete Hegseth, could face scrutiny.Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House, but conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority in the Senate.No party has held a two-thirds Senate majority since the mid-1960s, when Democrats briefly controlled 68 of the chamber’s 100 seats.Democratic Representative Al Green of Texas has repeatedly introduced resolutions seeking Trump’s impeachment during his second term, though his efforts have failed to advance.You use AI every day. articles.title: GOP lawmakers urge Rubio to weigh visa restrictions on corrupt officials as Albania rocked by protests
articles.summary: Two Republican Congressmen urge Marco Rubio to impose visa restrictions on corrupt Albanian officials as violent protests demand Edi Rama's resignation.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Two Republican members of Congress sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressing concern over the state of NATO ally Albania’s democratic backsliding, urging the department to use its visa restriction authority against Albanian officials complicit in significant corruption. "We write to express concern about the state of democracy and the rule of law in the Republic of Albania, a NATO ally and candidate for European Union membership. The United States has invested heavily in Albania's justice reforms and has a strong interest in their success. Recent events suggest that progress is fragile and, in key areas, at risk of reversal," the letter to Secretary Rubio said. Specifically, the letter urges Secretary Rubio to use the State Department's authority under Section 7031(c) of the annual Department of State, Foreign Operations and Related Programs Appropriations Act to publicly designate Albanian officials and their immediate family members, if necessary, if credible information of involvement in significant corruption exists. SERBIA’S LONGTIME LEADER FACES BIGGEST POLITICAL TEST AS STUDENTS MOUNT ELECTION CHALLENGE The letter, written by Rep. Joe Wilson, R-S.C., and his Republican colleague, House Europe Subcommittee Chairman Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, requested the administration answer four key questions by Nov. 5. In addition to asking the state department to commit to reviewing Albanian officials for designation under its visa restriction authority, the members of congress inquired about what assistance is being provided to Albania's broader justice reform efforts and whether the U.S. Embassy in Tirana is working with local officials to protect protesters and journalists. The Republican representatives are also requesting an update on former Deputy Prime Minister Belinda Balluku, who was charged with interfering in public procurement for road construction. Prosecutors asked parliament in December 2025 to lift her immunity so she could be arrested, but Prime Minister Edi Rama called the request unconstitutional, and parliament has not allowed the arrest to proceed. The members of congress say that Albania's anti-corruption institutions cannot succeed in rooting out corruption when political leaders shield the officials they investigate. US LAWMAKERS SOUND ALARM AS VIOLENCE GRIPS NATO ALLY ALBANIA AMID ANTI-GOVERNMENT PROTESTS Like fellow protesters in France and across Europe, tens of thousands have protested amid allegations of government corruption, inadequate education, unemployment and a lack of opportunity. The growing nationwide protest movement is driven by students and citizens also demanding accountability, an end to corruption and what they say is the restoration of democratic institutions and the rule of law. Demonstrations broke out in the capital, Tirana, two weeks ago, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. The protests quickly turned violent as demonstrators lobbed Molotov cocktails at the Education Ministry and clashed with police. Protesters also took aim at Rama’s Socialist Party headquarters in Tirana, squaring off with riot police who had been dispatched to protect government property. Rama blamed "foreign hands who do not want Albania in the European Union and who promote the masks that claim to represent students, but who in fact, more than students, represent organized crime itself." So far, the prime minister has refused to resign but has proposed entering into dialogue with the protesters. FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE The violence taking place across Albania is a worrying sign for a country struggling to maintain its democracy and continue the path to EU accession. "Congress is deeply concerned about the situation in Albania as the government uses excessive force against citizens who are demanding accountability and clean institutions. Corruption and narcotrafficking associated with the Rama government must be countered," Rep. Wilson told Fox News Digital in a statement. The turmoil in Albania comes as the country has long sought European Union membership, which began in 2014 when it became an official candidate for accession. While the 2025 annual European Commission report stated that Albania made significant strides in judicial reforms and combating organized crime, the continued allegations of corruption in the Rama government and the current violence taking place will complicate its path to EU membership. The student protests in Albania mirror the mass protests that took place in neighboring Serbia, where a student-led political movement toppled longtime leader Aleksandar Vučić. "Vucic’s defeat by a student-backed movement, following nearly two years of demonstrations over corruption and government accountability, is a striking parallel with the unrest now confronting Rama in Albania, where protests have been ongoing for over 150 days," Agim Nesho, former Albanian ambassador to the U.N. and U.S., told Fox News. articles.title: Embassy builder sues State Department for $461M
articles.summary: An Alabama-based construction company sued the State Department on Wednesday over accusations it refused to pay for pandemic-era cost overruns at a dozen embassy and consulate projects during the pandemic. BL Harbert International says the government had agreed to a settlement until political appointees under Secretary of State Marco Rubio inserted themselves into the process. “And, on…
articles.body:
An Alabama-based construction company sued the State Department on Wednesday over accusations it refused to pay for pandemic-era cost overruns at a dozen embassy and consulate projects during the pandemic.

BL Harbert International says the government had agreed to a settlement until political appointees under Secretary of State Marco Rubio inserted themselves into the process.

“And, on information and belief, the Government’s decision to renege on this heavily negotiated agreement with a long-trusted construction partner of the Department of State came from the top,” the lawsuit states.

The suit, filed in the Court of Federal Claims, seeks at least $461 million in damages.

The Hill has reached out to a State Department spokesperson for comment.

BL Harbert’s case concerns a dozen projects spread across the globe.

The company demands reimbursement for its construction of new embassies in Turkey, Guatemala, Montenegro, Namibia and Honduras as well as four consulates in Morocco, Thailand, Iraq and four in Mexico.

BL Harbert says the government had directed the company to continue work when the COVID-19 pandemic shut down normal life in 2020, driving up costs, and the State Department told it to submit adjustments.

Eventually, the government agreed in September 2025 to pay the company $370 million to settle the cost overruns, court documents show, and an initial payment of nearly $502,000 was made.

But BL Harbert says the Trump administration is now walking away from its deal.

It comes after The New York Times reported this summer that Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India, separately terminated the company’s work on a new embassy in New Delhi. Gor told the outlet that President Trump had personally approved the cancellation and it would save hundreds of millions of dollars.

“We did not want to take this step. The U.S. Government is an important partner, and we are proud of the work we do together to advance America’s interests and protect Americans serving overseas,” Charles Bohn, the company’s president, said in a statement.

“But we have a responsibility to our employees and to the future of that mission. We kept our commitment under extraordinarily difficult conditions. We are asking the government to keep its commitment to us.”

articles.title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
articles.summary: With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies are set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
articles.body:
Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.

Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.

Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.

With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from groups including soldiers, diplomats and hospital patients yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios

Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority

During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.

"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.

He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.

"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.

Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.

"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."

Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.

Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".

"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."

As the votes were counted on Wednesday, it emerged that his bloc had done better than the exit polls predicted and was on course to win 53 seats. However, that figure is 15 seats fewer than it had once controlled in the last Knesset.

Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hard-line, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.

Avigail Levine from Kfar Saba, who voted for former prime minister Naftali Bennett's opposition Beyachad party, told the BBC that she was disappointed with the election results.

"I was hoping for new leadership. I feel we need it as a nation," she said. "The people in power on 7 October should not be in power now."

She said people were frustrated that Netanyahu had not shouldered responsibility for what happened three years ago, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Her husband's grandmother was among those who died in Kibbutz Be'eri.

Gal from Ramat Gan said he voted for Netanyahu because Israelis "cannot relax and live in peace with neighbours when all they want is to erase us from the map".

He also said he was "afraid of the strengthening of the Arab political parties".

Likud complained on Wednesday that they had "stolen" the election. It alleged that they had resorted to "bribery, threats, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to encourage voters", without providing any evidence. The Central Elections Committee said it would examine the claims as part of a post-election review.

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - are set to almost double their representation because of a surge in turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Mahdi Kabaha who lives in a village near Haifa and campaigned to get out the Arab vote, described the result as "historic".

"Arab citizens came out and said clearly: we want a real say in this country," he said.

The head of the Joint List, Yousef Jabareen, told the BBC that Arab voters had been motivated in part by the opportunity to remove far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from office, whom he accused of racism and "provocation against our community".

Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party, has called for the annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians. Several Western countries have imposed sanctions on him for incitement against Palestinians.

United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".

The leader of the left-wing Democrats party, Yair Golan, told his partners in Eisenkot's bloc that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.

"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," he wrote on X.

Eisenkot has previously raised objections or attached conditions to that kind of alliance, including recognising Israel as Jewish and democratic, and Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must be destroyed. The right-wing parties in his bloc, meanwhile, have flatly rejected it.

"The opposition parties cannot dictate any conditions," Jabareen said. "If the opposition in Israel are willing to afford real and substantive change, and an alternative for the dangerous, extreme-right-wing government... they will have to negotiate with us."

articles.summary: At least two people were killed and five others critically injured after a gas bowser collided with another heavy vehicle and exploded in Pakistan's
articles.body: At least two people were killed and five others critically injured after a gas bowser collided with another heavy vehicle and exploded in Pakistan's southern Sindh province on Wednesday, police said.The accident occurred on the National Highway near Rohri Interchange in Sukkur district. Preliminary reports suggest the gas bowser, which was carrying fuel under pressure, collided at high speed with a heavy trailer.The impact damaged the bowser's tank, triggering a powerful explosion and a fire that spread to nearby vehicles, Xinhua News Agency reported.Police said the two people killed were the driver and cleaner of the gas bowser. Both died at the scene after being caught in the explosion.Rescue teams and emergency services rushed to the site after receiving reports of the blast. The five injured people, who suffered serious burns and other injuries, were taken to a nearby hospital in Sukkur for treatment. articles.title: New York Times editor admits paper should be more 'discerning' on labeling liberals
articles.summary: Law professor Jason Blackman challenged the New York Times over inconsistent use of conservative and liberal labels, and a top editor acknowledged it.
articles.body: A New York Times editor acknowledged during an interview on Thursday that the paper applied political labels to analysts and professors inconsistently after a law professor challenged the newspaper's decision to identify him as a conservative. Patrick Healy, the assistant managing editor for Standards and Trust at the Times, said during the "Sound Off" podcast that law professor Josh Blackman reached out after he was labeled a "conservative" in Times reporting twice within 24 hours. "Josh, you reached out after the Times twice described you as a, quote, conservative, end quote, law professor. And you said the conservative label was accurate, but that The Times applies labels like conservative and liberal inconsistently to law professors and analysts, and that a scholar’s view should speak for itself," Healy said. DEPARTURE OF NEW YORK TIMES COLUMNIST PUTS A SPOTLIGHT ON THE VOID OF PRO-TRUMP VOICES IN ITS OPINION PAGES Blackman described the issue as a longstanding grievance with all major media outlets and said he was quoted twice as a "conservative law professor" in New York Times articles in February. "I just thought that was strange. So I went through the Westlaw archives and just sort of searched for 'liberal' law professors and 'conservative' law professors in the New York Times database, and it was far more likely that you’re identifying a conservative than a liberal. And those numbers are stacked because liberals are quoted even more often. So the numbers even have a greater disparity," he said during the conversation with Healy. CONGRESS TO PUT AMERICAN BAR ASSOCIATION IN HOT SEAT OVER DEI RULES TIED TO LAW SCHOOL ACCREDITATION "And this sort of reinforces, I think, a perception that both the academy and, frankly, the media views a liberal position as a neutral position. And the conservative position is the other, the outlier. And that’s why you have to have this sort of nomenclature, this sort of adjective to describe it," Blackman said. He said he wrote a letter to the editor in February and the Times didn't publish it, but added that he appreciated Healy reaching out to him about it. LEGACY MEDIA TRUST HITS NEW LOW WITH SWALWELL STORY LATEST EXAMPLE OF PROTECTING DEMS Healy went on to acknowledge the validity of Blackman's critique: "I think there’s real truth to your critique and it’s something we need to do a better job on." "It can come off like The Times treats liberals as normal and conservatives as unique and worthy of labeling," Healy said. "In the legal academy, there are a lot of liberals, but that doesn’t justify it. I think we need to be more discerning about it." NEW YORK TIMES PROBES NICHOLAS KRISTOF COLUMNS AFTER REPORT HE FAILED TO DISCLOSE CAMPAIGN DONOR CONNECTIONS Fox News Digital reached out to the New York Times for comment. Blackman argued that the label should reflect a professor's involvement in an issue rather than their political affiliation. He said, "And some of your reporters have said, well, 'Professor Blackman has filed briefs in support of the Trump administration', or 'has filed a brief in opposition to the Obama administration on health care,' or, you know, 'has filed a brief in support of the Texas attorney general' — whatever it happens to be. That's actually a data point that's useful because it shows a person has sort of a dog in the fight." He said broad labels, such as conservative and liberal, don't tell the reader much. "So it presumes that, well, because he’s conservative, you know, you should discount his views supporting Trump, or conversely, because the person’s liberal, you should perhaps discount their views supporting President Obama or President Biden, whoever it happens to be. I would — if you’re trying to build up trust and standards, I would focus on the potential reason for a conflict or bias, and not just how the person identifies politically," Blackman said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Curtis Houck, a managing editor at NewsBusters, told Fox News Digital in a statement, "It seems like Healy is aiming to go to Halloween parties this weekend as Captain Obvious. It's one thing to recognize you have a problem, but as most people are aware, that's only step one, and it can often be used to punt or not actually follow through on changes." Houck added, "Healy, if pressed on camera, would probably try to back off or memory hole this conversation instead of making any concrete commitment to The Times doing any better. He's probably more upset that someone reached out to catch the paper red-handed instead of the fact that he — through his own journalism career — and his colleagues have spent more than a lifetime burying and/or smearing conservatives." The Wall Street Journal's assistant editor to the editorial page, James Freeman, praised the NYT in a piece on Monday, and credited them for acknowledging a source's criticism. articles.title: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions unanswered
articles.summary: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.
articles.body:
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.

It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.

While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.

The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.

Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%

However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.

The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.

As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.

The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.

There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.

And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.

Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.

Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.

And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.

Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.

So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.

With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.

The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.

So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.

For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.

A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

articles.title: What caused the deadly train crash in Spain? What we know so far
articles.summary: Scores of people were killed after two trains collided in Spain on Wednesday, in a crash that authorities say was caused by both computer system failure and apparent human error.
articles.body: Scores of people were killed after two trains collided in Spain on Wednesday, in a crash that authorities say was caused by both computer system failure and apparent human error. At least 68 people were killed and more than 100 injured after one train rear-ended another train near the town of Urda, in Toledo province, on the high-speed line that connects Madrid and Seville. One of the trains, operated by Spain’s national rail company Renfe, plowed into a stationary train operated by the private company Iryo, at a time when all train traffic in the area was disrupted due to a problem with the LZB train management safety system. It marks the third deadly rail incident in Spain this year, following a major crash in January in Córdoba province in which more than 40 people died, and a crash near Barcelona that killed a train driver. “Today, Spain is in mourning. All of Spain is in mourning,” said Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez from the scene of the crash on Wednesday, as he expressed his “full solidarity” with victims’ families. What caused the collision? Spain’s transportation minister Óscar Puente said that a computer system failure led to an issue with the safety system along a 63-kilometer (40-mile) stretch of track causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically. At that point, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, ADIF, took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound along the tracks despite a red light. The Renfe train was authorized to proceed without any speed restrictions due to an erroneous order from a train controller. As a result, Puente said that between 8:36 a.m. and 8:52 a.m. local time, it resumed traveling at about 124 miles per hour, eventually colliding with the stationary Iryo train. “There was a red signal prohibiting movement, yet the train was authorized to proceed,” the transportation minister said at a press conference on Wednesday. “It is a decision made under inexplicable circumstances.” Following Puente’s comments, Spanish trade union CSIF called on the transport minister to resign, saying: “We demand that the Government respect the investigation and the presumption of innocence for the head of traffic at ADIF.” CNN has approached Spain’s transport ministry for comment. Among those who were killed, 24 were on the Renfe train, traveling from Madrid to Seville, and 44 were on the Iryo train, also going between Madrid and Seville. Puente added that there will be a full investigation into the incident. Sánchez said that “if there has been negligence, it will come to light. And if there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness.” What have the passengers said? Passengers told CNN that the moment of the crash on Wednesday was “very chaotic,” and people were immediately thrown out of their seats and on top of one another inside the carriages. One surviving passenger said that three of the train cars in particular “were in terrible shape.” “One was on fire, in another there were people trapped and crying,” said the passenger, who declined to give her name. “And then in the main one (impacted) – there were people buried under debris.” Another passenger, Yoander, 25, said, “I was sleeping, and when I woke up I was already crashing into the seats in front of me.” “I hit my face and my leg,” he told CNN’s producer on the ground. “I’m in pain, but there are people that need more help than I do.” A woman who was traveling on the Renfe high-speed train also described “awful” scenes as people were thrown into the air. Speaking to CNN, Patricia said her train had been stopped for about 20 minutes before the accident, with an announcement explaining there was a lot of traffic. “After that, we departed, and maybe not after even three minutes, there was a crash,” she said. “Some people were hurled into the air… it was awful,” she said. “Some of the train structure got into our carriage, and our carriage wasn’t even the worst (affected).” There were 151 passengers on the Iryo train and 393 passengers on the Renfe train, according to the latest update from the regional government of Castilla and La Mancha. How have authorities responded? Dozens of fire trucks, ambulances, and police cars rushed to the site of the crash in the immediate aftermath. The Spanish civil guard set up multiple tents for what amounted to a huge emergency response, according to CNN’s team on the ground. More than 500 emergency personnel were deployed to the site of the crash to assist with rescue operations, Spain’s interior ministry said, as well as at least three helicopters and several drones. Emergency responders have been combing through the rubble of some of the heavily damaged carriages of the Iryo train. Several carriages of the state-owned Renfe high-speed train were tilted on their side after coming off the rails. Authorities moved passengers who did not have serious injuries away from the site via buses. Several passengers being bussed away had minor injuries, including cuts on their faces and around their eyes, and what appeared to be bloody noses. The evacuated passengers included citizens of multiple nationalities, including Spain, Brazil and elsewhere, according to CNN’s producer at the scene. The US State Department has said “several” Americans were injured in the train collision. The town of Urda, roughly five miles from the crash site, has received dozens of ambulances and emergency service vehicles, according to a second CNN team in the area. Red Cross workers operating out of the town’s sports center are treating the injured. The Spanish Civil Guard announced that they have opened four offices in different Spanish cities to swiftly identify the victims of the crash. Meanwhile, the regional government has urgently called for blood donations following the train crash, urging citizens to donate blood at sites in the cities of Alcázar de San Juan, Ciudad Real and Toledo. Rescue crews continued to search for anyone trapped in the wreckage on Wednesday evening under the glare of bright flood lights. What’s Spain’s rail safety record? Prime Minister Sánchez said on Wednesday that “it’s clear that we have suffered two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail in the same year,” acknowledging the other major crash in Córdoba province that killed more than 40 people in January. The crash on Wednesday happened about 130 miles from the site of the January train disaster near the town of Adamuz, along the same high-speed rail route that runs between Madrid and Seville. However, the cause of the train crash earlier this year was markedly different. That collision involved one train derailing due to a break in the track and crossing onto an adjacent track, according to Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE. Prior to the Adamuz train disaster, Spain’s train drivers’ union, Semaf, had raised concerns about high speeds causing vibrations and subsequent wear and tear along high-speed railway lines, a source from the union told CNN at the time. A third crash this year near Barcelona – which happened days after the Adamuz train disaster – involved a commuter train derailing on a day of heavy rainfall. That crash killed the driver and injuring dozens of passengers, according to the regional government of Catalonia at the time. The successive incidents have raised concerns about Spain’s railway infrastructure, computer systems and the maintenance of both. But prior to this year, European Union statistics show that Spain’s rail safety record was better than many other European countries. In 2023, Spain had fewer than 1 railway deaths per one million inhabitants – giving it the best record in the EU at the time, according to a Eurostat report. Most railway deaths in the EU are a result of unauthorized people on the tracks, rather than incidents that kill passengers or staff inside the train, data shows. CNN’s Catherine Nicholls, Michael Rios, Billy Stockwell and Jack Guy contributed to this report.
