articles.title: ​A Texas barber was $100 short on rent when he spotted a bag containing $128,514 left near an ATM; newly released police body-camera footage shows how he contacted officers and helped return the cash
articles.summary: What would you do if you found a bag containing $128,514 left unattended at an ATM?
articles.body: What would you do if you found a bag containing $128,514 left unattended at an ATM? A 37-year-old barber in Lewisville, Texas, walked up to a Bank of America ATM on West Main Street on August 3. He was about $100 short on rent and had spent part of that day arguing about it. Sitting on top of the machine were two bags; one contained $128,514 in cash, while the other held 19 cheques, according to NBC 5. Faced with a sum that could have covered his rent many times over, he made a choice few would expect. He chose honesty over free money.He wasn’t excited to see the money. Fear came before anything else. In the body-camera footage, the man tells Officer J. Nazario how he felt when he saw the money. ​"Bro, you know what I felt when I saw it? I got scared, bro,​" he said, according to CBS News. He started shaking and asked himself what he should do. He called the police immediately. He also told the officer that he had a felony on his record. Police said the man and his 42-year-old friend had found the two bags, one of which contained $128,514.A bag left behindThe bags appeared to have been left behind by a Brink’s crew servicing the Bank of America ATM. The man found a label on one of the bags pointing to a Chick-fil-A down the road. They went there looking for the owner, but the restaurant did not claim the money. The owner explained that a nearby business, now operating as Hawaiian Bros, had previously been a Chick-fil-A. The ATM apparently still carried identification linked to the former restaurant. The owner then contacted the police.Police arriveWhen Officer Nazario reached the scene, he could hardly believe the amount. The officers counted the cash, and a bank receipt inside the bag listed exactly $128,514. Nothing was missing. Detective Gina Miller of the Lewisville Police Department said she had handled cases involving people returning wallets, identification and other lost property, but had never seen someone turn in that much cash. ​"I’ve never had somebody turn in that kind of money before,​" she told the broadcaster.The barber, however, revealed the circumstances behind his financial difficulties. ​"I'm arguing with her at the Walmart because I'm short on rent,​" he recalled. ​"Go to the ATM, I'm short 100.​" That’s when he found the money. ​"I started shaking. I'm like, what do I do? I called the laws.​"The cash went into the department’s property room. Bank of America told the channel that it was grateful for the man’s actions, but did not say whether he had received any money. Although the police did not give him a reward, they expressed their appreciation for his actions.​"It takes a lot to do the right thing. And I can't commend you enough. Especially, like you said, in this day and age, that's impressive,​"​ the officer said. Although the man wanted to avoid public attention, he confirmed that he would attend a private ceremony if the police department honoured him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: After decades collecting artworks from colonial-era India, British historian Charles Greig has donated 50 paintings and watercolours to Tate, including rare 18th-century portraits; a public display is planned for 2028
articles.summary: A painting is never merely a record of truth, but a subject of representation and reimagination.
articles.body: A painting is never merely a record of truth, but a subject of representation and reimagination. And artworks specially prepared while recording the British colonial period in India are not merely art, but a glimpse into an India that exists today only in a few inches of frame. This is particularly true of artworks created in India during the 18th and 19th centuries, when British colonial expansion was changing the political and cultural landscape of the subcontinent. According to the Art Newspaper and a press release attributed to Tate, a collection of 50 such works has now found a permanent home at Tate in London, following a donation by British art historian Charles Greig, who spent over 4 decades bringing them together.The collection includes paintings, watercolours and miniatures by Indian and European artists who lived and worked in India. The works offer different perspectives on the period, from portraits of Indian figures to landscapes that record places during a time of considerable change. A free public display featuring works from the collection is planned at Tate Britain in 2028, giving visitors an opportunity to explore a part of art history shaped by the relationship between Britain and India.A collection built over four decadesGreig assembled the collection over approximately 45 years, developing an interest in the ways artists represented India and how the people of the pivoting colonial period was preserved in art. His decision to donate the works to Tate reflects his belief that a collection built through years of research should be accessible to the public rather than remain in private hands.Through myriad textures, strokes and frames, the paintings coalesce names that must be familiar to students of art history and others whose contributions have been widely recorded and recognised. Among the artists represented are Indian painters Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan, alongside European artists Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, with the British landscape painters Thomas Daniell and William Daniell also featured in the collection.The donation includes three watercolours by Sita Ram, an Indian artist who worked for British patrons during the early 19th century. His paintings are associated with the tradition known as Company painting, which developed as Indian artists responded to demand from officials and other patrons connected with the British East India Company. Among the other notable works is Johan Zoffany's Portrait of Prince Jawan Bakht, painted in 1784. The portrait illustrates an Indian royal figure through the work of a European artist at a time when the balance of power was changing in the subcontinent.Another fascinating work, is Rudolf Swoboda's painting of a sepoy in HH Maharaja Srinagar's IndianRegiment, painted around 1886. The work has come to form part of the collection's record of people who lived under British rule and provides a visual point of reference for understanding the period's military and social structures.What the paintings reveal about colonial IndiaThe historical value of the collection lies not only in the artists who created the works but also in the different perspectives they bring together. Some paintings were produced by European artists working in India, while others were made by Indian artists responding to new forms of patronage. Together, they offer a way to examine how people, landscapes and cultural practices were represented during a period shaped by colonial power. But at the same time, the collection makes room for Indian artists whose work developed within these changing circumstances. Their presence is important to a fuller understanding of the period, as the history of art in colonial India cannot be told solely through the experiences of European painters who travelled to the subcontinent.Greig has described the works as a visual record of a world that existed before photography became widely established. Their depictions of people and places can help researchers and visitors engage with historical settings through the details preserved on canvas and paper.A new chapter for the collectionThe donation also expands Tate's holdings of art connected with Anglo-Indian history. The institution already has works associated with this period, including Zoffany's Colonel Mordaunt's Cock Match, painted around 1784, as well as Indian landscapes by British artists. Greig's collection adds to this material, allowing the museum to present a broader account of the artistic relationships that developed between Britain and the Indian subcontinent.For Greig, the decision to donate the works was closely tied to the question of who should be able to see and study them. He has described himself as a temporary steward of the collection, emphasising the importance of preserving the artworks together and making them available beyond a private audience.When the works go on display at Tate Britain in 2028, visitors will be able to encounter these paintings within a public museum setting, where their artistic qualities can be considered alongside the histories that shaped their creation.
